summary: Single-author design manual for ATWZ, a filesystem-based operations layer (skills, hooks, scripts) around Claude Code's Agent Teams. It keeps each agent's role, checkpoints, decisions, and inbox messages in per-agent 'workstation' directories so that a team can be rebuilt with one command after a session ends or compaction. The author states it is a design manual, not an empirical study, and reports no measurements.

claims.claim: ATWZ lets an interrupted Claude Code agent team be restored with a single command and recovers working state lost to compaction.
claims.evidence: Mechanism described in §6.1-6.4 (checkpoints, reactivation for CC >= 2.1.178 and earlier versions). No recovery-reliability measurement; §1 and §12 explicitly say 'We make no benchmarking or user-study claims' and 'we have not measured how much they help'.

claims.claim: File-based state substantially mitigates agentic 'technical debt' and reduces prompt-writing effort through inter-agent document passing.
claims.evidence: Abstract asserts 'substantially mitigate' and 'greatly reducing the effort'; the body offers only design rationale (§4.2, §7) and scenarios, with no comparison against alternatives.

claims.claim: The design was hardened through real use, and a catalog of failure modes with mitigations was found.
claims.evidence: §10.1 lists about 9 anecdotal incidents (ghost respawns, timezone false alarm, archival buck-passing, releases missing migration scripts) with fixes. Self-reported, from using the layer to build itself; §10.2 says the list is not exhaustive.

patterns.note: Per-agent persistent state in files (workstations, checkpoints); no evaluation.
Argues compaction erodes working detail; uses file checkpoints to recover after compaction. Asserted, not measured.
Role library and team-lead/teammate protocol on top of Claude Code Agent Teams (§8).
Lead decomposes and delegates to teammates.
File inbox doubles as an audit trail of which agent did what (§7).
Human kept in the loop throughout; no gate evaluation.
Installer writes rule blocks into CLAUDE.md and README; describes rule drift across installed copies (§10.1).

methodology.sample: None. Self-use while building the tool itself.
methodology.models: Claude Code (versions before and from 2.1.178); no model-level reporting.
methodology.languages: Shell/scripts layer; target projects not characterized.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint (31 pages, 9 figures); no venue.

biases.detail: All failure-mode evidence comes from the author's own use; there is no external user.
Abstract says 'substantially mitigate' and 'greatly reducing the effort' even though §12 says nothing was measured.
Design manual only; recovery reliability and overhead are untested.
Tightly coupled to Claude Code Agent Teams internals that already changed once (v2.1.178), so the design is fragile to vendor API churn. §2.3 notes Codex lacks equivalent persistent teams.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Builds on Anthropic Claude Code; the author's own open-source tool.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding section found.
coi.detail: No vendor affiliation. The 'GitHub' vendor hit comes from the arXiv page boilerplate. The author describes and promotes their own tool, but no comparative claim is made.

verdict_reason: Admit only as a design reference for a file-backed persistence pattern. It has no evaluation at all, and every benefit claim is unsupported by the authors' own admission (§1, §12).
applicability: The transferable idea for the Java team is host-neutral: store agent working state (decisions, checkpoints, hand-off documents) as committed or workspace files rather than chat context. This matches the team's handoff-by-commit rule and suits mixed agent hosts and spec-driven development, since hand-off documents can be spec fragments. The implementation itself is Claude-Code-specific (Agent Teams API, hooks), so it would not carry over to Codex, Hermes, or Cursor hosts, and it has no notion of coordinating across 4+ ingestion repositories. Treat it as a pattern sketch, not evidence. The failure catalog (§10.1), especially release migrations missing and rules not reaching subagents, is a useful checklist of things that go wrong when stamping rule files.
